briefs.openingParagraph:
NDT reporting software replaces clipboard-and-Word report production with structured field capture on a tablet, automatic report generation from that captured data, and a reviewed, signed PDF delivered to the client in the same shift. In the United States it exists to make inspection records defensible under ASME BPVC Section V, API 510, API 570, API 653 and AWS D1.1 audit.

A US inspection company running six technicians typically loses four to five hours per technician per month to report formatting alone, before a single client revision. The bottleneck is structural, not clerical: readings are written on a field sheet, photographs sit on a technician's phone, calibration records live in a separate binder, and a Word template is retyped for every job. NDT reporting software removes the retyping step by making the field capture form the report source. The technician records thickness readings, indication locations, probe and couplant details, and calibration block identification against a job that already carries the client, asset, procedure and acceptance criteria. Report generation then becomes a render, not an authoring task, and the ASNT Level III reviewer signs an artifact whose data provenance is traceable to the shift it was captured on.

briefs.h1: How to Get OmniScan, Epoch and Phased Array Instrument Data Into a Client-Deliverable Inspection Report
briefs.openingParagraph:
Getting OmniScan or Epoch data into a client report is a two-stage problem, because the instrument file and the deliverable are different objects. Stage one is export: OmniScan X3 writes .nde, older OmniScan MX and SX write .opd, and Epoch series flaw detectors export datalogger files and screen captures. Stage two is placement: the exported image, reading table or C-scan must land inside a report that also carries calibration, procedure and technician certification records.

There is no DICOM equivalent in NDT. Unlike medical imaging, which standardised on a single interchange format decades ago, ultrasonic and phased array instruments write proprietary containers that only their own analysis software fully reads — WeldSight and OmniPC for Evident, UltraVision and Capture for Eddyfi, UltraVision for Zetec. Evident's Open File Format NDE is the closest thing to a neutral container and is readable through a published HDF5-based schema, which is why .nde is the practical target for any export workflow built after 2021. Everything else routes through a CSV or image export step. The consequence for report production is that the instrument vendor solves analysis and stops; nobody in the reporting software category solves the handoff, which is why this question is answered today only on ndt.net forum threads.

briefs.h1: NDT Reporting in Excel and Word vs Dedicated Software: Where Spreadsheets Break, and the Reading Count Where They Stop Working
briefs.openingParagraph:
Excel and Word are adequate for NDT reporting up to roughly 20 reports a month with two or three technicians and a single report format. Spreadsheets break at four specific points: when two technicians edit the same workbook, when a client requests a format change that must be applied retrospectively, when an auditor asks which procedure revision a 14-month-old report was written against, and when thickness readings must be trended across inspection cycles rather than reported once.

The failure is not that Excel calculates wrongly. It is that a spreadsheet holds no relationships. A corrosion monitoring location that appears in a 2024 workbook, a 2025 workbook and a 2026 workbook is three unrelated cells, so remaining-life calculation under API 510 and API 570 becomes manual re-keying, and a transcription error in that re-keying is invisible. There is no record of who changed a value after review, which is the exact question an API-authorised inspector asks during a turnaround audit. And because the template carries no procedure version, a report cannot be tied to the revision of the written procedure in force on the day of the test, which ASME BPVC Section V Article 1 expects the record to establish.

briefs.h1: Offline NDT Inspection Apps: What Genuinely Works With No Signal, How Sync Resolves Conflicts, and When a Report Can Be Signed On Site
briefs.openingParagraph:
Three different things are sold as offline NDT inspection, and only one of them survives a refinery turnaround. Cached read-only forms let a technician view a job without signal but not record against it. Offline capture with queued sync records readings locally and uploads on reconnect. Full offline operation additionally generates and signs the finished PDF on the device, so the client receives the report before the crew leaves the site. Ask any vendor which of the three it does, in those words.

The distinction decides real jobs. Inside a tank, under insulation on a pipe rack, on an offshore platform, or in a plant that blocks personal devices on its wireless network, connectivity is absent for the whole shift, not intermittently. A queued-sync system is adequate there because the data is captured locally and reconciled later, but the client will not have the report on site. A signed-on-site system removes a whole business day from the invoicing cycle, which is why it is the criterion most repeated across every vendor in this category. The engineering constraint behind all of it is conflict resolution: when two technicians capture against the same asset offline and both reconnect, the system must merge by record rather than overwrite by timestamp, or one technician's shift silently disappears.

briefs.h1: Build vs Buy NDT Reporting Software: The Four Costs In-House Builds Underestimate, and the Three Cases Where Building Is Actually Right
briefs.openingParagraph:
Building in-house NDT reporting software is the right decision in three situations: the inspection workflow is genuinely proprietary and is itself the commercial differentiator, the company already runs a permanent software team maintaining production systems, or a regulatory or customer constraint forbids data leaving a specific environment. Outside those three, buying wins — not on build cost, which teams estimate reasonably well, but on maintenance cost, which they almost never model.

The four costs that get omitted are code drift, method drift, platform drift and departure risk. Code drift is continuous: ASME BPVC publishes on a two-year cycle, API 510, API 570 and API 653 issue addenda and errata between editions, and every one of those can change what a compliant record must contain. Method drift means each new method or instrument the company adopts requires new capture forms and new validation. Platform drift means iOS and Android releases break offline capture roughly annually. Departure risk is the sharpest: an internally built reporting system usually has one author, and when that person leaves, an inspection company discovers it now owns a software product it cannot modify but cannot stop using, because every client report for five years was generated by it.

briefs.openingParagraph:

It maps at the functional location or asset record, at the notification or work order that triggered the inspection, and at the measurement point where a thickness reading becomes a measurement document. It breaks at the evidence layer: neither system has a native place for a calibration certificate, a DAC curve, a radiograph, an IQI record or a technician certification reference, so those must live in the reporting platform and be referenced by URL, not copied.

That asymmetry determines the correct architecture. SAP PM and Maximo are systems of record for the asset and the work; a reporting platform is the system of record for the inspection evidence. Pushing every field into the CMMS produces an unusable asset master and loses the evidence anyway; keeping everything in the reporting platform strands the reading data outside the reliability workflow that needs it. The working pattern is to push the structured measurement — measurement point, reading, unit, date, technician identifier, procedure reference — and to reference the report document by stable URL. Power BI then reads the measurement series for corrosion rate and remaining-life trending under API 510 and API 570, while the report itself remains one click away and fully auditable.

briefs.h1: NDT Report Templates by Code: What ASME Section V, API 510, API 570, API 653 and ISO 9712 Each Require the Report to Contain
briefs.openingParagraph:
ASME BPVC Section V requires an NDT record to identify the procedure and its revision, the technique details for the method used, the personnel who performed the examination and their qualification level, the equipment and its calibration, the examination conditions, and the results including the acceptance criteria applied. API 510, API 570 and API 653 add the in-service dimension: condition monitoring locations, measured thickness, corrosion rate, remaining life and the next inspection date.

ISO 9712 governs the certification of the person, not the content of the report, and this is the most common confusion in this area. A report is not ISO 9712 compliant; the technician is ISO 9712 certified, and the report records that certification alongside the examination. In the United States the equivalent personnel framework is ASNT SNT-TC-1A, an employer-based recommended practice under which the employer's own written practice defines qualification, or ASNT CP-189 where a standard rather than a recommended practice is required. A report template that carries the wrong personnel framework for its market fails audit on a paperwork technicality rather than on any inspection deficiency, which is why the template set below is separated by code rather than by method alone.

briefs.h1: NDT Personnel Certification Tracking Software: Managing SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, ISO 9712, PCN and NAS 410 Expiries Across One Workforce
briefs.openingParagraph:
ANSWER BLOCK (immediately under the H1 — 69 words): "NDT personnel certification tracking software holds every technician's qualification record — scheme, method, level, certifying authority, issue date, expiry date, annual vision examination and the specific written practice or standard it was certified under — and alerts before each lapses. In the United States the complication is that one technician commonly holds certifications under two or three schemes at once: employer-based under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, third-party under ASNT's own programme or ISO 9712, and NAS 410 for aerospace work."

SECOND BLOCK (still above the fold, 158 words): "Those schemes do not share a renewal calendar or a renewing authority, which is why a spreadsheet fails at scale. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies the technician against the employer's own written practice, and the recommended practice ties recertification to a defined interval with an annual near-vision and colour-contrast examination throughout. ASNT CP-189 is a standard rather than a recommended practice and is invoked contractually, so an employer working to it cannot simply write its own looser rules. ISO 9712 certification is issued by an independent certification body, not the employer, so the employer cannot renew it — it can only track it and give notice. NAS 410 governs aerospace NDT personnel and is referenced by prime contractors directly. The audit exposure is not the lapse itself; it is a report signed by a technician whose certification had expired on the examination date, discovered months later during a client audit of a completed job."

SECTION 1 — DECOMPOSITION TABLE (the page's core asset, within the first 40% of the page). <caption>NDT personnel certification schemes: who certifies, renewal basis and what the employer must retain</caption>. 6 rows x 6 columns. Rows: ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ASNT CP-189, ASNT third-party certification programme, ISO 9712, PCN (BINDT), NAS 410 / EN 4179. Columns: Scheme | Certifying authority | Level II renewal basis | Vision examination requirement | Record the employer must retain | Who can sign the certification. This is the axis no aggregator and no software vendor publishes, and it is the reason this page can be cited.

SECTION 2 — 'The multi-scheme problem' (~300 words). One worked technician record: a Level II holding UT and MT under an employer written practice to SNT-TC-1A, PT under ISO 9712 through a certification body, and an aerospace endorsement under NAS 410 for one client. Show the four different expiry dates, the four different renewal actions, and who is responsible for each. Present as a small table.

SECTION 3 — 'What actually goes wrong' — five failure modes, each 120-160 words, each self-contained: (1) technician assigned to a job after expiry; (2) vision examination lapsed while the certification is current; (3) written practice revised but existing certifications not re-mapped; (4) certification held but not for the specific method/technique the procedure requires; (5) records held by a former employer and not reconstructable.

SECTION 4 — 'What the system must do' — eight capability H3s, 100-150 words each: per-scheme expiry rules; alert lead times by scheme; block or warn on assignment of an unqualified technician; store scanned certificates and examination results; link the qualification record to each report the technician signed; hold vision examination dates separately; produce an audit pack for one technician on demand; report workforce coverage by method and level.

briefs.h1: NDT Equipment Calibration Tracking Software: Due Dates, Recall Intervals and Traceability for UT Gauges, Phased Array Probes, MPI Yokes and Densitometers
briefs.openingParagraph:
ANSWER BLOCK (immediately under the H1 — 67 words): "NDT equipment calibration tracking software records every instrument, probe, block and accessory a contractor owns, its calibration or verification interval, the date last performed, the certificate and its traceability to a national standard, and the technician or laboratory that performed it — then recalls the asset before it goes out of date. Search results for this term return calibration laboratories, not software; the two are different purchases and this page covers the software side."

SECOND BLOCK (still above the fold, 154 words): "The reason contractors need it is that NDT assets do not share one interval. A magnetic particle yoke requires a lifting-force check under ASTM E1444 and ASTM E709 at defined intervals and again after any repair or damage. A penetrant line requires system checks under ASTM E1417. A radiographic densitometer requires verification against a calibrated step wedge at intervals stated in the written procedure and referenced by ASME BPVC Section V, Article 2. An ultrasonic instrument requires linearity checks per ASME BPVC Section V, Article 5 and its referenced practices, while the transducer itself has its own verification history. Aerospace work under NAS 410 adds its own traceability expectations. A single spreadsheet column called 'next due' cannot carry rules that differ per asset class, and it cannot prove traceability of the reference standard used — which is the specific record an assessor asks to see."
outline: H1 + both answer blocks. Keep existing module copy; additive only.

SECTION 1 — 'Calibration laboratory vs calibration tracking software' (~200 words). Explicitly disambiguates the SERP: Trescal, Tektronix, Tra-Cal and similar perform the calibration; tracking software holds the schedule, the certificate and the traceability chain. Naming the confusion is what makes this the correct answer to the query.

SECTION 2 — DECOMPOSITION TABLE (within the first 40% of the page). <caption>NDT asset classes: verification activity, governing reference and record retained</caption>. 8 rows x 5 columns. Rows: ultrasonic flaw detector; ultrasonic thickness gauge; phased array instrument and probe; magnetic particle yoke; magnetic particle bench/coil; penetrant line and materials; radiographic densitometer and step wedge; eddy current instrument and probe. Columns: Asset | Verification or calibration activity | Governing reference (ASTM/ASME/manufacturer) | Typical interval basis | Record that must be retained. State that intervals are set by the employer's written procedure and the governing code, not by this page — do not invent universal intervals.

SECTION 3 — 'Traceability: the record most spreadsheets cannot produce' (~250 words). Chain from the instrument, to the reference block or standard used, to that standard's own certificate, to the national measurement standard. Reference ISO/IEC 17020 equipment requirements and ISO/IEC 17025 where the contractor also runs a lab.

SECTION 4 — Six capability H3s, 120-160 words each: asset register with serial numbers and owner; per-class interval rules; automatic recall with configurable lead time; block assignment of an out-of-calibration asset to a live job; link the asset used to the specific report produced; hold the certificate PDF with its traceability reference.

SECTION 5 — 'The two-way link nobody builds' (~200 words). Certification tracking answers 'was the technician qualified'; calibration tracking answers 'was the equipment in date'. A client audit asks both about the same report. The system must resolve report -> technician qualification -> equipment calibration in one query. This is the page's differentiating argument and links to the certification page.

In a spreadsheet, the certification list and the report are two unlinked artefacts, and the spreadsheet has usually been edited since. ISO/IEC 17020 adds control-of-records and control-of-documents obligations that an unversioned workbook on a shared drive does not meet. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer's written practice is itself a controlled document, and if the written practice has been revised since a certification was issued, the spreadsheet has no way to show which revision applied. The six findings below follow directly from those three documents."

briefs.h1: Offline Mobile NDT Data Capture: How Field Records Stay Audit-Defensible When There Is No Signal
briefs.openingParagraph:
ANSWER BLOCK (immediately under the H1 — 67 words): "An offline NDT data capture app stores readings, photographs and sign-offs on the device with no connection and synchronises them when the technician returns to coverage. The capability that matters is not offline storage — every vendor claims it — but what happens at sync: how conflicting edits are resolved, which timestamp is retained on the record, and whether the resulting audit trail would survive a client audit of the completed job."

SECOND BLOCK (still above the fold, 155 words): "Offline capture surfaced as the single most repeated buyer requirement in this market, yet no vendor has published a page on how it actually works. That gap matters because offline capture creates a specific compliance risk: the record is written on a device whose clock the technician can change, is edited before anyone else sees it, and arrives in the system hours or days after the examination. If the system stores only the sync time, the report shows an examination date that cannot be independently supported. If it stores only the device time, the date is trivially alterable. A defensible design retains both, records which was used, and marks any record where they diverge beyond a set tolerance. The same reasoning applies to photographs: an image without a retained capture timestamp and a hash taken at capture is evidence of nothing once it has passed through a phone gallery."
outline: H1 + both answer blocks.

SECTION 1 — 'Where offline capture is actually needed' (~200 words). Concrete US contexts: refinery turnarounds inside vessels and behind steel, pipeline right-of-way, offshore platforms, tank farms, aerospace hangars with restricted-device policies. Name the constraint in each — no signal, no personal device permitted, intrinsically safe equipment required.

SECTION 2 — DECOMPOSITION TABLE: <caption>Offline capture: what breaks at sync, and the control that resolves it</caption>. 6 rows x 4 columns. Rows: two technicians edit the same work order; supervisor edits in the office while the technician is offline; device clock incorrect; photograph added from gallery rather than camera; report signed offline then data amended; device lost before sync. Columns: Scenario | What a weak system does | What a defensible system does | Record retained.

SECTION 3 — 'Timestamp integrity' (~300 words). Device clock vs server clock vs network-derived time, which one goes on the record, and how divergence is flagged. State that the examination date on an NDT report is a substantive field, not metadata, because it is the date against which the examiner's certification currency is judged under ASNT SNT-TC-1A and against which equipment calibration status is judged.
SECTION 4 — 'Photograph chain of custody' (~250 words). Capture-time hashing, retained EXIF, camera-only capture versus gallery import, and why an assessor treats them differently.

SECTION 5 — 'Conflict resolution strategies' (~300 words) — last-write-wins, field-level merge, and explicit conflict queue — with a plain statement of which is acceptable for inspection records and why last-write-wins is not.
SECTION 6 — 'What to test in a demo' — six numbered tests the buyer can run, including putting the device in airplane mode mid-form and forcing a two-device conflict.

SECTION 7 — Six question-headed H2s with self-contained answers: 'How long can a device stay offline?'; 'What happens if the device is lost before sync?'; 'Can a technician sign a report offline?'; 'Does offline capture work on iOS and Android?'; 'Do intrinsically safe tablets run these apps?'; 'When is offline capture unnecessary?'
SECTION 8 — FAQ, 6 pairs. CTA: 'Request a demo'. No price.

thesis: This segment has 110 pages and 17 clicks because every page is written to the same buyer everyone else writes to — the plant-owner CIO shopping for a platform — and Atlantis has no authority in that fight. The win is to abandon the platform-buyer SERP and own the NDT-to-twin data intersection, where the only occupants are TechCorr (3,800 words, zero tables, zero FAQ), a ResearchGate figure caption and an ndt.net PDF, and where an ASNT Level III byline is the one credential no content farm or SaaS vendor can fabricate. briefs.openingParagraph:

Ultrasonic testing supplies wall thickness at fixed condition monitoring locations. Phased array supplies gridded C-scan corrosion maps. Radiography supplies weld flaw position and type. Magnetic particle and liquid penetrant supply coordinate-pinned surface indications. Eddy current supplies tube bundle maps. TOFD supplies crack height for API 579 assessment."

EXPANSION BLOCK (still above the fold, immediately below): "In the United States the layer that carries commercial weight is the ultrasonic thickness layer, because API 510 for pressure vessels and API 570 for piping both set inspection intervals from measured corrosion rate and calculated remaining life, not from calendar age. Phased array adds coverage: a UT spot reading gives one number, while an encoded PAUT C-scan gives a thickness surface, which is what an API 579 local thin area assessment requires. Radiography, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant and eddy current contribute event data rather than continuous fields — a specific indication, at a coordinate, on a date, with a disposition. A usable twin must carry both data shapes."

briefs.h1: Digital Twin vs IDMS (Inspection Data Management System) — What Each Actually Does, Where They Overlap, and Whether You Need Both
briefs.openingParagraph:
ANSWER BLOCK: "An IDMS stores and trends inspection data: CML registers, thickness histories, corrosion rates, risk rankings and next-due dates. A digital twin attaches that same data to a geometric model of the asset. The IDMS answers what was measured and when the next inspection is due. The twin answers where it is, what condition it is in now, and what the next turnaround has to cover."

EXPANSION BLOCK: "Most US refiners and chemical plants already run an IDMS, and the practical question is never replacement — it is whether the twin sits on top of the IDMS, beside it, or absorbs it. The deciding factor is where the corrosion rate calculation lives. Under API 510 and API 570, inspection intervals are set from measured corrosion rate and calculated remaining life, and whichever system performs that calculation becomes the system of record for compliance. Running the calculation in two places produces two next-due dates and fails an audit. The workable pattern for a plant with an existing IDMS is to keep the IDMS as the calculation authority and the CML register master, and let the twin read from it for visualisation, scan planning, scaffold and access planning, and turnaround scope. A greenfield operator with no IDMS can start with a twin that carries the register natively."

briefs.title: DICONDE & ISO 15926: NDT Data Handover to a Digital Twin
briefs.h1: DICONDE, ISO 15926 and the Standards That Govern NDT Data Handover Into a Digital Twin
briefs.openingParagraph:
ANSWER BLOCK: "DICONDE, defined by ASTM E2339, is the DICOM-derived standard that stores an NDT image together with its acquisition metadata in one file, so a radiograph or an ultrasonic scan carries its technique, calibration and asset identity with it. ISO 15926 covers the plant data model that image must attach to. A digital twin needs both: DICONDE for the evidence, ISO 15926 for the address."

EXPANSION BLOCK: "The practical consequence is that exporting inspection data to CSV or PDF destroys the part a twin most needs. A PDF report proves an inspection happened; it cannot tell a model which component was scanned, at what gain, with which probe, against which calibration block, on which date. DICONDE keeps those attributes bound to the data, which is why it matters for digital radiography and computed radiography in particular — the ASTM family extends the base practice to specific modalities, with separate parts covering ultrasonic, digital radiographic and computed tomographic data. ISO 15926 solves the other half: it standardises how plant equipment, its parts and its lifecycle information are represented so that a scanning contractor, an IDMS vendor and a twin platform can exchange the same asset breakdown structure without a bespoke mapping project for every handover."
